title: Feedback Loops — The Universal Regulator
description: Feedback loops govern everything from thermostats to economies: negative feedback stabilizes (a deviation corrects itself), positive feedback amplifies (a deviation grows). Cybernetics, endocrinology, and climate science all run on the same diagram — sensor, comparator, effector — applied to different substrates. Find the loop and you find the leverage: change the gain, the delay, or the goal, and the system's behavior transforms.

title: Supply and Demand — The Universal Price Signal
description: Wherever trade happens, price carries information: scarcity raises price, surplus lowers it, and the intersection rations goods to those who value them most. The pattern holds for tulips, GPUs, apartments, and kidneys (where price is banned, queues and favors become the currency). Interventions that ignore it — price caps, bans — don't repeal it; they move the cost elsewhere.

title: Network Effects — Metcalfe's Universal
description: A network's value grows with the square of its users — Metcalfe's law — which is why telephones, social platforms, and marketplaces tip to winner-take-most. The same math governs languages, standards, and cities: each new node makes every existing node more valuable. It also explains fragility: lose the critical mass and the value collapses quadratically.

description: Symmetry dictates physical law: Noether proved every continuous symmetry yields a conservation law — time symmetry gives energy conservation, rotational symmetry gives angular momentum. It is the closest thing science has to an aesthetic that turned out to be true.

title: Least Action — Nature's Laziness
description: Light, planets, and quantum particles all extremize action — nature is 'lazy' in a precise mathematical sense. Fermat's least time gives Snell's law; the principle of least action gives all of classical mechanics; Feynman's path integral sums over all paths weighted by action. One variational principle, nearly all of physics.

title: Emergence — More Is Different
description: Anderson's 1972 thesis: at each level of complexity, new properties appear that the parts don't have — wetness from H2O molecules, consciousness from neurons, markets from traders. Reduction explains the parts; emergence explains the wholes. It is why psychology isn't applied biology and economics isn't applied psychology — each level needs its own laws.
